subject: math
title: Grade 4 Perimeter
seo_title: Grade 4 Perimeter Worksheets: Free Math Practice with Answer Key (BC Curriculum)
standard_text: Perimeter of regular and irregular shapes
meta_desc: Free Grade 4 math worksheets on perimeter for the BC curriculum: count sides on a grid, multiply for regular polygons, use 2 × length + 2 × width for rectangles, find a missing side, and solve composite shape and garden fence word problems. 100 questions with an answer key, good FSA numeracy practice.
key_big: Perimeter is the distance all the way around a shape: add every side.
key_sub: Regular polygon: side × number of sides. Rectangle: 2 × length + 2 × width. Count the sides, not the squares inside, and change to one unit first (2 m = 200 cm).
body_html:
What is perimeter?

Perimeter is the distance all the way around a flat shape. To find it, add every side. Perimeter is a length, so it uses mm, cm, m or km.

Regular polygons: multiply

In a regular polygon, every side is the same length. Perimeter = side length × number of sides.

Rectangles: 2 lengths and 2 widths

A rectangle has 4 sides, even when only 2 numbers are shown. Perimeter = 2 × length + 2 × width.

Example 1: find a missing side

A rectangle has a perimeter of 30 cm. It is 9 cm long. How wide is it?

The two lengths use 2 × 9 = 18 cm. 30 − 18 = 12 cm is left for the two widths. 12 ÷ 2 = 6.

Answer: 6 cm

Composite shapes

Some shapes are made of rectangles. Use the sides you know to find the missing ones. Then add every side.

Example 2: use the same unit

A garden bed is 2 m long and 40 cm wide. What is its perimeter?

Change first: 2 m = 200 cm. Then 200 + 40 + 200 + 40 = 480.

Answer: 480 cm

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Counting the squares insideThat is the area. Perimeter counts the sides around the outside
Adding only the 2 numbers shown on a rectangleAdd all 4 sides: 9 + 4 + 9 + 4
Missing a short side on an L shapeCount the sides first, then add that many numbers
Using 4 sides for every shapeA hexagon has 6 sides, an octagon has 8
Adding 2 m + 40 cm as 42Change to one unit first: 200 cm + 40 cm

faq.q: What do Grade 4 students learn about perimeter in BC?
faq.a: In the Geometry and measurement area of the BC Grade 4 math curriculum, students find the perimeter of regular and irregular shapes using standard units like mm, cm and m.

faq.q: What is the formula for the perimeter of a rectangle?
faq.a: Perimeter = 2 × length + 2 × width. A rectangle 9 cm long and 4 cm wide has a perimeter of 18 + 8 = 26 cm.

faq.q: How do you find a missing side when you know the perimeter?
faq.a: Add the sides you know, then subtract that total from the perimeter. For a rectangle, take away the two lengths and halve what is left to get the width.

faq.q: Do these perimeter worksheets help with the Grade 4 FSA?
faq.a: Yes. The Grade 4 FSA includes numeracy, where students solve problems in real situations. Word problems like fencing a garden or walking a trail are good practice for that kind of thinking.

sets.title: Perimeter on a grid: count and add the sides

items.q: What is perimeter?
c: the length of the longest side
the distance all the way around a shape
the number of squares inside a shape
items.e: Perimeter is the distance around the outside edge. The squares inside show the area, not the perimeter.

items.q: Each small square is 1 cm on each side. What is the perimeter of the rectangle?
items.e: Count the 1 cm sides all the way around: 4 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 14 cm. There are 12 squares inside. That is the area, not the perimeter.

items.q: Each small square is 1 cm on each side. What is the perimeter of the rectangle?
items.e: Count the 1 cm sides all the way around: 6 + 2 + 6 + 2 = 16 cm. There are 12 squares inside. That is the area, not the perimeter.

items.q: Each small square is 1 cm on each side. What is the perimeter of the square?
items.e: Count the 1 cm sides all the way around: 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20 cm. There are 25 squares inside. That is the area, not the perimeter.

items.q: Each small square is 1 cm on each side. What is the perimeter of the rectangle?
items.e: Count the 1 cm sides all the way around: 2 + 5 + 2 + 5 = 14 cm. There are 10 squares inside. That is the area, not the perimeter.

items.q: Each small square is 1 cm on each side. What is the perimeter of the rectangle?
items.e: Count the 1 cm sides all the way around: 7 + 3 + 7 + 3 = 20 cm. There are 21 squares inside. That is the area, not the perimeter.

items.q: Each small square is 1 cm on each side. What is the perimeter of the rectangle?
items.e: Count the 1 cm sides all the way around: 8 + 3 + 8 + 3 = 22 cm. There are 24 squares inside. That is the area, not the perimeter.

items.q: Each small square is 1 cm on each side. What is the perimeter of the shape?
items.e: Start at one corner and go around the outside, counting every 1 cm side: 18 cm. Count the short steps too. The 14 squares inside are the area.

items.q: Each small square is 1 cm on each side. What is the perimeter of the shape?
items.e: Start at one corner and go around the outside, counting every 1 cm side: 20 cm. Count the short steps too. The 13 squares inside are the area.

items.q: Each small square is 1 cm on each side. What is the perimeter of the shape?
items.e: Start at one corner and go around the outside, counting every 1 cm side: 12 cm. Count the short steps too. The 5 squares inside are the area.

items.q: Each small square is 1 cm on each side. What is the perimeter of the shape?
items.e: Start at one corner and go around the outside, counting every 1 cm side: 20 cm. Do not forget the sides that go in and out. The 13 squares inside are the area.

items.q: Each small square is 1 cm on each side. What is the perimeter of the shape?
items.e: Start at one corner and go around the outside, counting every 1 cm side: 16 cm. Count the short steps too. The 10 squares inside are the area.

items.q: Each small square is 1 cm on each side. What is the perimeter of the shape?
items.e: Start at one corner and go around the outside, counting every 1 cm side: 18 cm. Count the short steps too. The 12 squares inside are the area.

items.q: Each small square is 2 cm on each side. What is the perimeter of the rectangle?
items.e: There are 12 small sides around the outside. Each one is 2 cm: 12 × 2 = 24 cm. 12 cm forgets that each side is 2 cm, not 1 cm.

items.q: Each small square is 2 m on each side. What is the perimeter of the shape?
items.e: Count the small sides around the outside: 12. Each one is 2 m: 12 × 2 = 24 m.

items.q: This is a plan of a school garden. Each square is 1 m on each side. How long is the fence all the way around it?
items.e: Count the 1 m sides around the outside: 20 m. 16 is the number of squares inside, which is the area of the garden.

items.q: Which shape has the longer perimeter?
items.e: A: 4 + 2 + 4 + 2 = 12 units. B: count around the outside, including the step: 12 units. They are the same.

items.q: Which shape has the longer perimeter?
items.e: A: 6 + 1 + 6 + 1 = 14 units. B: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12 units. So A is longer around, even though B has more squares inside (9 vs 6). More squares means more area, not always more perimeter.

items.q: What is the perimeter of this triangle?
items.e: Add all 3 sides: 7 + 13 + 15 = 35 cm.

items.q: What is the perimeter of this shape?
items.e: Add all 4 sides: 10 + 7 + 14 + 7 = 38 m. Touch each side as you add it so you do not skip one.

sets.title: Regular polygons: side length × number of sides

items.q: All the sides of this equilateral triangle are the same length. What is its perimeter?
items.e: An equilateral triangle has 3 equal sides. Multiply: 3 × 8 = 24 cm. Not every shape has 4 sides: 8 × 4 = 32 is wrong here.

items.q: All the sides of this square are the same length. What is its perimeter?
items.e: A square has 4 equal sides. Multiply: 4 × 9 = 36 cm. 9 × 9 = 81 would be the area, not the perimeter.

items.q: All the sides of this regular pentagon are the same length. What is its perimeter?
items.e: A regular pentagon has 5 equal sides. Multiply: 5 × 6 = 30 cm. Not every shape has 4 sides: 6 × 4 = 24 is wrong here.

items.q: All the sides of this regular hexagon are the same length. What is its perimeter?
items.e: A regular hexagon has 6 equal sides. Multiply: 6 × 7 = 42 cm. Not every shape has 4 sides: 7 × 4 = 28 is wrong here.

items.q: All the sides of this regular octagon are the same length. What is its perimeter?
items.e: A regular octagon has 8 equal sides. Multiply: 8 × 5 = 40 cm. Not every shape has 4 sides: 5 × 4 = 20 is wrong here.

items.q: All the sides of this equilateral triangle are the same length. What is its perimeter?
items.e: An equilateral triangle has 3 equal sides. Multiply: 3 × 15 = 45 m. Not every shape has 4 sides: 15 × 4 = 60 is wrong here.

items.q: All the sides of this square are the same length. What is its perimeter?
items.e: A square has 4 equal sides. Multiply: 4 × 25 = 100 cm. 25 × 25 = 625 would be the area, not the perimeter.

items.q: All the sides of this regular pentagon are the same length. What is its perimeter?
items.e: A regular pentagon has 5 equal sides. Multiply: 5 × 12 = 60 m. Not every shape has 4 sides: 12 × 4 = 48 is wrong here.

items.q: All the sides of this regular hexagon are the same length. What is its perimeter?
items.e: A regular hexagon has 6 equal sides. Multiply: 6 × 20 = 120 mm. Not every shape has 4 sides: 20 × 4 = 80 is wrong here.

items.q: All the sides of this regular octagon are the same length. What is its perimeter?
items.e: A regular octagon has 8 equal sides. Multiply: 8 × 11 = 88 cm. Not every shape has 4 sides: 11 × 4 = 44 is wrong here.

items.q: All the sides of this regular hexagon are the same length. What is its perimeter?
items.e: A regular hexagon has 6 equal sides. Multiply: 6 × 35 = 210 cm. Not every shape has 4 sides: 35 × 4 = 140 is wrong here.

items.q: All the sides of this regular pentagon are the same length. What is its perimeter?
items.e: A regular pentagon has 5 equal sides. Multiply: 5 × 45 = 225 m. Not every shape has 4 sides: 45 × 4 = 180 is wrong here.

items.q: What is a regular polygon?
c: All its sides are different lengths.
All its sides and all its angles are equal.
items.e: A regular polygon has all sides the same length and all angles the same size, like a square or a regular hexagon. So its perimeter = side length × number of sides.

items.q: A regular hexagon has sides of 9 cm. Which number sentence gives its perimeter?
items.e: A hexagon has 6 sides, each 9 cm. Add 9 six times, or multiply: 6 × 9 = 54 cm.

items.q: A sign is shaped like a regular octagon. Each side is 30 cm. What is the perimeter of the sign?
items.e: An octagon has 8 sides: 8 × 30 = 240 cm. 120 cm uses only 4 sides, and 210 cm leaves out one side.

items.q: A square floor tile has sides of 15 cm. What is the perimeter of the tile?
items.e: A square has 4 equal sides: 4 × 15 = 60 cm. 225 is 15 × 15, the area.

items.q: An equilateral triangle has sides of 1 m. What is its perimeter in centimetres?
items.e: 1 m = 100 cm. 3 sides: 3 × 100 = 300 cm. 3 cm forgets to change metres to centimetres.

items.q: A regular hexagon has sides of 50 cm. What is its perimeter in metres?
items.e: 6 × 50 = 300 cm. 100 cm = 1 m, so 300 cm = 3 m. 300 m mixes up cm and m.

items.q: Which has the longer perimeter: a square with 10 cm sides or a regular pentagon with 8 cm sides?
items.e: Square: 4 × 10 = 40 cm. Pentagon: 5 × 8 = 40 cm. They are the same. 100 is the area of the square, and 48 uses 6 sides for the pentagon.

items.q: A regular hexagon and a square both have 6 cm sides. How much longer is the hexagon’s perimeter?
items.e: Hexagon: 6 × 6 = 36 cm. Square: 4 × 6 = 24 cm. 36 − 24 = 12 cm. The hexagon has 2 more sides, and 2 × 6 = 12.

items.q: What is the perimeter of the rectangle?
items.e: A rectangle has 2 lengths and 2 widths: 2 × 9 + 2 × 4 = 18 + 8 = 26 cm. 9 + 4 = 13 is only two of the four sides.

items.q: What is the perimeter of the rectangle?
items.e: A rectangle has 2 lengths and 2 widths: 2 × 12 + 2 × 7 = 24 + 14 = 38 m. 12 + 7 = 19 is only two of the four sides.

items.q: What is the perimeter of the rectangle?
items.e: A rectangle has 2 lengths and 2 widths: 2 × 15 + 2 × 6 = 30 + 12 = 42 cm. 15 + 6 = 21 is only two of the four sides.

items.q: What is the perimeter of the rectangle?
items.e: A rectangle has 2 lengths and 2 widths: 2 × 20 + 2 × 9 = 40 + 18 = 58 cm. 20 + 9 = 29 is only two of the four sides.

items.q: What is the perimeter of the rectangle?
items.e: A rectangle has 2 lengths and 2 widths: 2 × 25 + 2 × 14 = 50 + 28 = 78 m. 25 + 14 = 39 is only two of the four sides.

items.q: What is the perimeter of the rectangle?
items.e: A rectangle has 2 lengths and 2 widths: 2 × 36 + 2 × 18 = 72 + 36 = 108 cm. 36 + 18 = 54 is only two of the four sides.

items.q: What is the perimeter of the rectangle?
items.e: A rectangle has 2 lengths and 2 widths: 2 × 48 + 2 × 25 = 96 + 50 = 146 m. 48 + 25 = 73 is only two of the four sides.

items.q: What is the perimeter of the rectangle?
items.e: A rectangle has 2 lengths and 2 widths: 2 × 120 + 2 × 65 = 240 + 130 = 370 m. 120 + 65 = 185 is only two of the four sides.

items.q: This is a square. What is its perimeter?
items.e: All 4 sides of a square are equal: 4 × 11 = 44 cm.

items.q: This is a square. What is its perimeter?
items.e: All 4 sides of a square are equal: 4 × 16 = 64 m.

items.q: Which gives the perimeter of a rectangle that is 8 cm long and 5 cm wide?
items.e: There are 2 lengths of 8 cm and 2 widths of 5 cm: 2 × 8 + 2 × 5 = 16 + 10 = 26 cm. 8 × 5 is the area.

items.q: Liam says the perimeter of a rectangle 10 cm long and 3 cm wide is 13 cm. What mistake did he make?
c: He added only 2 of the 4 sides.
items.e: 10 + 3 = 13 uses one length and one width. The rectangle has 4 sides: 10 + 3 + 10 + 3 = 26 cm.

items.q: Ava says a rectangle 6 m long and 4 m wide has a perimeter of 24 m. What did she find?
items.e: 6 × 4 = 24 is the number of square metres inside: the area. The perimeter is 6 + 4 + 6 + 4 = 20 m.

items.q: What is the perimeter in centimetres?
items.e: The units are different. Change first: 2 m = 200 cm. Then 2 × 200 + 2 × 40 = 400 + 80 = 480 cm. Adding 2 + 40 + 2 + 40 = 84 mixes m and cm.

items.q: What is the perimeter in centimetres?
items.e: The units are different. Change first: 3 m = 300 cm. Then 2 × 300 + 2 × 75 = 600 + 150 = 750 cm. Adding 3 + 75 + 3 + 75 = 156 mixes m and cm.

items.q: What is the perimeter in centimetres?
items.e: The units are different. Change first: 1 m = 100 cm. Then 2 × 100 + 2 × 25 = 200 + 50 = 250 cm. Adding 1 + 25 + 1 + 25 = 52 mixes m and cm.

items.q: What is the perimeter in millimetres?
items.e: The units are different. Change first: 12 cm = 120 mm. Then 2 × 120 + 2 × 45 = 240 + 90 = 330 mm. Adding 12 + 45 + 12 + 45 = 114 mixes cm and mm.

items.q: A school field is a rectangle 125 m long and 80 m wide. What is its perimeter?
A classroom rug is a rectangle 350 cm long and 275 cm wide. What is its perimeter?
A farm field in the Fraser Valley is a rectangle 2400 m long and 1600 m wide. What is its perimeter?

sets.title: Find the missing side from the perimeter

items.q: The perimeter of this triangle is 29 cm. What is the missing side length?
items.e: Add the sides you know: 7 + 10 = 17. Subtract from the perimeter: 29 − 17 = 12 cm. Check: 7 + 10 + 12 = 29.

items.q: The perimeter of this triangle is 31 m. What is the missing side length?
items.e: Add the sides you know: 11 + 7 = 18. Subtract from the perimeter: 31 − 18 = 13 m. Check: 11 + 7 + 13 = 31.

items.q: The perimeter of this triangle is 27 cm. What is the missing side length?
items.e: Add the sides you know: 5 + 10 = 15. Subtract from the perimeter: 27 − 15 = 12 cm. Check: 5 + 10 + 12 = 27.

items.q: The perimeter of this quadrilateral is 53 m. What is the missing side length?
items.e: Add the sides you know: 14 + 17 + 11 = 42. Subtract from the perimeter: 53 − 42 = 11 m. Check: 14 + 11 + 17 + 11 = 53.

items.q: The perimeter of this quadrilateral is 63 cm. What is the missing side length?
items.e: Add the sides you know: 16 + 17 + 15 = 48. Subtract from the perimeter: 63 − 48 = 15 cm. Check: 16 + 15 + 17 + 15 = 63.

items.q: The perimeter of this quadrilateral is 49 m. What is the missing side length?
items.e: Add the sides you know: 13 + 9 + 9 = 31. Subtract from the perimeter: 49 − 31 = 18 m. Check: 13 + 9 + 18 + 9 = 49.

items.q: The perimeter of the rectangle is 30 cm. How wide is it?
items.e: The two lengths use 2 × 9 = 18 cm. That leaves 30 − 18 = 12 cm for the two widths. Each width is 12 ÷ 2 = 6 cm.

items.q: The perimeter of the rectangle is 46 cm. How wide is it?
items.e: The two lengths use 2 × 15 = 30 cm. That leaves 46 − 30 = 16 cm for the two widths. Each width is 16 ÷ 2 = 8 cm.

items.q: The perimeter of the rectangle is 64 m. How wide is it?
items.e: The two lengths use 2 × 20 = 40 m. That leaves 64 − 40 = 24 m for the two widths. Each width is 24 ÷ 2 = 12 m.

items.q: The perimeter of the rectangle is 100 m. How wide is it?
items.e: The two lengths use 2 × 35 = 70 m. That leaves 100 − 70 = 30 m for the two widths. Each width is 30 ÷ 2 = 15 m.

items.q: A rectangle has a perimeter of 54 cm. It is 7 cm wide. How long is it?
items.e: The two widths use 2 × 7 = 14 cm. 54 − 14 = 40 cm for the two lengths. Each length is 40 ÷ 2 = 20 cm. Check: 20 + 7 + 20 + 7 = 54.

items.q: A square has a perimeter of 36 cm. How long is each side?
items.e: A square has 4 equal sides: 36 ÷ 4 = 9 cm. Check: 4 × 9 = 36. Dividing by 2 gives 18, which is two sides together.

items.q: A square has a perimeter of 84 m. How long is each side?
items.e: A square has 4 equal sides: 84 ÷ 4 = 21 m. Check: 4 × 21 = 84. Dividing by 2 gives 42, which is two sides together.

items.q: A square has a perimeter of 200 cm. How long is each side?
items.e: A square has 4 equal sides: 200 ÷ 4 = 50 cm. Check: 4 × 50 = 200. Dividing by 2 gives 100, which is two sides together.

items.q: An equilateral triangle has a perimeter of 36 cm. How long is each side?
items.e: An equilateral triangle has 3 equal sides: 36 ÷ 3 = 12 cm. Check: 3 × 12 = 36. Dividing by 4 only works for a square.

items.q: A regular hexagon has a perimeter of 48 cm. How long is each side?
items.e: A regular hexagon has 6 equal sides: 48 ÷ 6 = 8 cm. Check: 6 × 8 = 48. Dividing by 4 only works for a square.

items.q: A regular octagon has a perimeter of 72 m. How long is each side?
items.e: A regular octagon has 8 equal sides: 72 ÷ 8 = 9 m. Check: 8 × 9 = 72. Dividing by 4 only works for a square.

items.q: Which rectangle has a perimeter of 28 cm?
items.e: 8 + 6 + 8 + 6 = 28 cm. Quick check: length + width must be half of 28, which is 14. 4 cm by 7 cm has an area of 28, not a perimeter of 28.

items.q: Which rectangle has a perimeter of 40 m?
items.e: 12 + 8 + 12 + 8 = 40 m. Quick check: length + width must be half of 40, which is 20. 5 m by 8 m has an area of 40, not a perimeter of 40.

items.q: Which rectangle has a perimeter of 50 cm?
items.e: 15 + 10 + 15 + 10 = 50 cm. Quick check: length + width must be half of 50, which is 25. 5 cm by 10 cm has an area of 50, not a perimeter of 50.

items.q: This is the shape of a deck. What is its perimeter?
items.e: Add all 6 sides: 9 + 3 + 5 + 5 + 4 + 8 = 34 m. An L shape has 6 sides, so check that you added 6 numbers.

items.q: What is the perimeter of this shape?
items.e: There are 8 sides: 12 + 3 + 4 + 6 + 4 + 6 + 4 + 3 = 42 cm. Count the sides first so you do not miss a short one.

items.q: What is the perimeter of this shape?
items.e: Add all 8 sides: 3 + 5 + 7 + 5 + 3 + 8 + 13 + 8 = 52 m. The notch adds two 5 m sides, so the answer is more than the 42 m of a plain 13 m by 8 m rectangle.

items.q: Simran’s family grows vegetables in Kelowna. Their garden is a rectangle 9 m long and 6 m wide. How much fence do they need to go all the way around it?
items.e: The fence goes around all 4 sides: 9 + 6 + 9 + 6 = 30 m. 15 m is only two sides, and 54 is the area.

items.q: Mateo’s family walks the trail around a lake in Stanley Park. The trail map shows 4 parts: 350 m, 280 m, 400 m and 220 m. How long is the whole loop?
items.e: Add all 4 parts: 350 + 280 = 630, 630 + 400 = 1030, 1030 + 220 = 1250 m. 1030 m leaves out the last part.

items.q: A hockey rink is about 60 m long and 26 m wide. About how long are the boards all the way around it?
items.e: 2 × 60 + 2 × 26 = 120 + 52 = 172 m. 86 m is one length and one width, and 1560 is the area.

items.q: For the Terry Fox Run, Grade 4 runs laps around the school field. The field is 120 m long and 80 m wide. How many laps make 2 km?
items.e: One lap: 120 + 80 + 120 + 80 = 400 m. 2 km = 2000 m. 400 × 5 = 2000, so 5 laps. 10 laps would be right only if one lap were 200 m (just 120 + 80).

items.q: The Stanley Park lake loop is 1250 m. How does that compare with 1 km?
items.e: 1 km = 1000 m. 1250 − 1000 = 250, so the loop is 250 m more than 1 km.

items.q: Chloe’s family builds a raised garden bed out of cedar boards. It is 240 cm long and 120 cm wide. How many centimetres of board go around the edge?
items.e: 2 × 240 + 2 × 120 = 480 + 240 = 720 cm. 600 cm leaves out one short side.

items.q: Kai’s garden bed is 3 m long and 80 cm wide. How much edging goes around it?
items.e: Change to the same unit first: 3 m = 300 cm. 300 + 80 + 300 + 80 = 760 cm. 166 cm comes from adding 3 + 80 + 3 + 80, which mixes metres and centimetres.

items.q: A park in Surrey is shaped like a triangle. Its sides are 140 m, 95 m and 115 m. Nadia walks once around the park. How far does she walk?
items.e: Add the 3 sides: 140 + 95 = 235, 235 + 115 = 350 m. 235 m leaves out the 115 m side.

items.q: Harjot builds a dog run 12 m long and 5 m wide. One long side is the wall of the house, so it needs no fence. How much fence does he need?
items.e: Only 3 sides get fence: 5 + 12 + 5 = 22 m. 34 m puts fence along the house wall too.

items.q: A square patio in Nanaimo has a perimeter of 28 m. How long is each side?
items.e: A square has 4 equal sides: 28 ÷ 4 = 7 m. 14 m is half of 28, which is two sides together.

items.q: Owen uses 34 m of fence to go around a rectangular chicken run. The run is 11 m long. How wide is it?
items.e: Two lengths: 11 + 11 = 22 m. 34 − 22 = 12 m for the two widths. 12 ÷ 2 = 6 m. 23 m forgets the second length.

items.q: Ms. Grewal’s bulletin board is 150 cm long and 90 cm wide. She has 4 m of paper border. Is that enough to go all the way around?
items.e: Perimeter: 150 + 90 + 150 + 90 = 480 cm. 4 m = 400 cm, and 400 < 480, so it is not enough. 240 cm is only one length and one width.

items.q: All the corners are square corners. Find the two missing sides. What is the perimeter?
items.e: The top is 12 cm, so the bottom part is 12 − 5 = 7 cm. The left side is 9 cm, so the short side is 9 − 5 = 4 cm. Now add all 6 sides: 12 + 5 + 7 + 4 + 5 + 9 = 42 cm. 31 cm adds only the 4 numbers shown.

items.q: A garden bed has steps on one side. All the corners are square corners. What is its perimeter?
items.e: The steps that go across add up to the 9 m side, and the steps that go up add up to the 6 m side. So the perimeter is the same as a 9 m by 6 m rectangle: 9 + 6 + 9 + 6 = 30 m.

items.q: Garden A is 10 m by 4 m. Garden B is 8 m by 7 m. Which garden needs more fence to go around it?
items.e: A: 10 + 4 + 10 + 4 = 28 m. B: 8 + 7 + 8 + 7 = 30 m. 30 − 28 = 2, so B needs 2 m more. 16 compares the areas (56 and 40), not the fences.

items.q: Ji-woo walks around a city block in Victoria 3 times. The block is 200 m long and 150 m wide. How far does he walk in all?
items.e: One time around: 200 + 150 + 200 + 150 = 700 m. 3 times: 3 × 700 = 2100 m. 1050 m uses only 200 + 150 for each lap.

items.q: Ryan puts a string of lights around a rectangular window. The window is 120 cm wide and 90 cm tall. How long is the string of lights?
items.e: 120 + 90 + 120 + 90 = 420 cm. 100 cm = 1 m, so 420 cm = 4 m 20 cm. 42 m mixes up centimetres and metres.
